_source: Every string below is copied verbatim from thrivingincollege.org, captured 2026-09-11. Do not reword, tighten or 'improve' any of it. The prose is a validated instrument's published description and a research audience checks it against the literature. The one editorial decision taken is recorded in ALPHA_CONFLICT.md: where the instrument page and /surveys publish different per-scale coefficients, the instrument page wins.

instruments.label: Undergraduate
instruments.name: Undergraduate Thriving Quotient
instruments.description: The Thriving Quotient undergraduate instrument: what it measures, its scales, how administration works, sample items, and what a campus survey costs.
instruments.capsule: The Undergraduate Thriving Quotient™ (TQ) is a reliable (α = .89), valid instrument that was developed to measure the academic, social, and psychological aspects of undergraduate students’ college experience that are most predictive of academic success, institutional fit, satisfaction with college, and ultimately graduation.
instruments.scales_intro: The 24 items on the TQ cluster onto five scales:

scales.name: Engaged Learning
scales.def: A measure of the degree to which students are meaningfully processing what happens in class and energized by what they are learning.
scales.sample: I feel energized by the ideas I am learning in most of my classes.

scales.name: Academic Determination
scales.def: A measure of students’ goal-directedness, investment of effort, and regulation of their own learning and use of time.
scales.sample: I am confident I will reach my educational goals.

scales.name: Positive Perspective
scales.def: A measure of students’ optimism and explanatory style.
scales.sample: I look for the best in situations, even when things seem hopeless.

scales.name: Social Connectedness
scales.def: A measure of students’ involvement in healthy relationships and social support networks, whether on or off campus.
scales.sample: I feel like my friends really care about me.

scales.name: Diverse Citizenship
scales.def: A measure of students’ desire to make a difference in the community around them, as well as their openness to differences in others.
scales.sample: I value interacting with people whose viewpoints are different from my own.

instruments.pathways_intro: Examining thriving among college students developed out of a desire to understand student success more holistically than previous higher education research that had focused solely on student retention. Dr. Laurie Schreiner developed the Thriving Quotient™ (TQ) using concepts from positive psychology (i.e., flourishing) and Bean and Eaton’s (2000) retention model to introduce the term thriving to “describe the experiences of college students who are fully engaged intellectually, socially, and emotionally” (Schreiner, 2010, p. 4). Thriving is not about personality traits, but rather describes malleable qualities within a student, meaning that institutions can teach students to thrive. Years of TQ research has documented specific experiences that serve as significant pathways to student thriving; these pathways are also measured in the online survey:

pathways.name: Sense of Community
pathways.def: A measure of student belonging, ownership, and sense of mattering to the institution.
pathways.sample: I feel like I belong here.

pathways.name: Institutional Integrity
pathways.def: A measure of the degree to which students perceive the institution to be “delivering on its promises.”
pathways.sample: This institution was accurately portrayed during the admissions process.

pathways.name: Spirituality
pathways.def: A measure of the degree to which students have a sense of meaning and purpose in their life that provides strengths during difficult times.
pathways.sample: My spiritual or religious beliefs provide me with a sense of strength when life is difficult.

pathways.name: Faculty Sensitivity to Diverse Learners
pathways.def: A measure of students’ perceptions of faculty inclusion of multiple perspectives in their curriculum and pedagogy, as well as their sensitivity to the needs of diverse learners.
pathways.sample: How satisfied are you with the degree to which your instructors include diverse perspectives in the curriculum?

pathways.name: Frequency of Student-Faculty Interaction
pathways.def: A measure of how often students interact with faculty in various settings or around academic or career/grad school plans.
pathways.sample: How often this year have you interacted with your instructors outside of class?

pathways.name: Satisfaction with Faculty Interactions
pathways.def: A measure of students’ satisfaction with how often they interact with faculty as well as quality of those interactions.
pathways.sample: How satisfied are you with the quality of the interactions you have had with your instructors so far this year?

pathways.name: Campus Involvement
pathways.def: A measure of students’ frequency of participation in campus activities, events, and organizations.
pathways.sample: How often this year have you participated in campus organizations?

instruments.closing: In addition to these predictive pathways, the instrument assesses students’ satisfaction with learning, advising, peer interactions, their living situation, mental and physical health, and overall satisfaction with their college experience. The TQ also measures the degree to which students are certain of their major, as well as demographic characteristics such as gender, age, race/ethnicity, household income, generation status, high school GPA, class level, athlete status, whether they live on campus, hours per week they work, and whether the institution was their first choice at enrollment. Target group reports can be requested on any of these demographic characteristics to determine whether thriving levels are significantly different across subpopulations of students.
citations: Schreiner, L. A. (2010c). The “Thriving Quotient”: A new vision for student success. About Campus, 15 (2), 2-10.

instruments.label: Sophomore
instruments.name: Sophomore Experiences Survey
instruments.population: students in their second year of college
instruments.description: The Sophomore Experiences Survey: what it measures, its scales, how administration works, sample items, and what a campus survey costs.
instruments.capsule: The Sophomore Experiences Survey (SES) is an online survey whose foundation is the Thriving Quotient, a reliable (α = .89), valid instrument that was developed to measure the academic, social, and psychological aspects of undergraduate students’ college experience that are most predictive of academic success, institutional fit, satisfaction with college, and ultimately graduation. Additionally, the survey contains scales predictive of thriving, as well as items specific to the sophomore experience. Intended for students in their second year of college, the SES provides institutions with actionable information about how their sophomores have experienced the university during this pivotal year, with national norms targeting only students in their second year. Typical administration of the survey occurs in February-March each spring.

Dr. Laurie Schreiner developed the Thriving Quotient™ (TQ) using concepts from positive psychology (i.e., flourishing) and Bean and Eaton’s (2000) retention model to introduce the term thriving to “describe the experiences of college students who are fully engaged intellectually, socially, and emotionally” (Schreiner, 2010, p. 4). pathways.name: Spirituality

instruments.closing: In addition to these predictive pathways, the online survey assesses sophomore-specific items, such as how often students have participated in any sophomore programming at their university, the extent to which they have participated in service-learning courses or learning communities, and how they have experienced their sophomore classes and entire experience compared to their first year of college. Target group reports can be requested on any of these demographic characteristics to determine whether thriving or satisfaction levels are significantly different across subpopulations of sophomores.

instruments.capsule: The Community College Student version of the Thriving Quotient contains the same scales as the original Thriving Quotient, but its items have been adapted to more accurately reflect the experiences of students in the community college setting.
instruments.closing: Research by Dr. Amy Azul at Victor Valley Community College in southern California
instruments.notes: The community college instrument's own page states that it carries the same scales as the original Thriving Quotient with items adapted to the community college setting. It publishes no coefficients, definitions or sample items of its own, and none are reproduced here from another instrument: the adapted item set has not been published, and a campus research office would check any figure shown against the literature. The five scale names and definitions are on the Undergraduate Thriving Quotient page.

instruments.label: Faculty
instruments.name: Faculty Thriving Quotient
instruments.description: The Faculty Thriving Quotient: what it measures, its scales, how administration works, sample items, and what a campus survey costs.
instruments.capsule: The Faculty Thriving Quotient (FTQ) is an instrument developed to assess the vital engagement of full-time faculty in their role. The Faculty Thriving Quotient is a valid and reliable (α = .94) instrument that assesses faculty flourishing in five dimensions: Meaningful Engagement, Institutional Affinity, Relational Support, Student Impact, and Affirmed Value. Attention to the predictors and campus elements supportive of faculty thriving can enable institutional leaders to more effectively serve their students by supporting their faculty.
instruments.scales_intro: The 21 items on the FTQ cluster onto 5 scales:

scales.name: Meaningful Engagement
scales.def: A measure of the degree to which faculty are energized by their work, experience positive emotions doing faculty work, and find meaning and purpose in their accomplishments and in the faculty role.
scales.sample: I feel energized by my work as a faculty member here.

scales.name: Institutional Affinity
scales.def: A measure of the degree to which faculty enjoy being at their particular institution, believe their values are aligned with the mission of the institution, feel like they belong at the institution, are proud to represent the institution in the broader academic community, and would stay at the institution if offered an equivalent position elsewhere.
scales.sample: I feel like I belong here.

scales.name: Relational Support
scales.def: An indicator of the positive relationships faculty have with their faculty colleagues and staff coworkers, along with the degree to which they feel supported and valued in those relationships.
scales.sample: I feel valued by my faculty colleagues.

scales.name: Student Impact
scales.def: A measure of the degree to which faculty believe they make a difference in students’ lives and enjoy working with students.
scales.sample: I enjoy my work with students.

scales.name: Affirmed Value
scales.def: A measure of the degree to which faculty believe their immediate supervisor cares about them, along with whether they have received positive feedback from their supervisor in the last year. Immediate supervisor is defined as their program director, department chair, or dean.
scales.sample: My immediate supervisor (department chair, program director, or dean) cares about me as a person.

instruments.pathways_intro: Faculty play a pivotal role in student learning, success, and thriving. Yet faculty often respond to data on student thriving with questions about how students can thrive if faculty themselves are not thriving. Examining thriving among faculty developed out of a desire to understand the faculty experience beyond productivity and satisfaction, as well as to provide institutions with actionable feedback on how to improve the experiences of their faculty so that students could learn and thrive. Dr. Laurie Schreiner (Azusa Pacific University) and Dr. Tami Martinez (Indiana University-South Bend) developed the Faculty Thriving Quotient (FTQ) using concepts from positive psychology (e.g., flourishing) and positive organizational scholarship. Faculty thriving reflects not only what a faculty member does in their faculty role, but also their relationship to the institution where they work and the ways in which they interact with others in that space that bring joy and a sense of meaning and purpose. Research on faculty thriving has discovered that there are specific experiences that serve as significant pathways to thriving in the faculty role. The online instrument assesses these pathways, as well:

pathways.name: Trusted Leadership
pathways.def: The strongest contributor to faculty thriving, this scale assesses trust in leadership, as well as support from leadership, effective communication within the institution, leaders’ commitment to faculty well-being, faculty voice in institutional decision-making, whether faculty perceive leaders to be competent, and optimism about the vision and future of the institution.
pathways.sample: There is a solid sense of trust between the faculty and administrators here.

pathways.name: Equitable Environment
pathways.def: A measure of the degree to which faculty feel they are free from stigmatization or discrimination, as well as their perception of the institution’s support and commitment to diverse perspectives and equity.
pathways.sample: Faculty are treated equitably at this institution, regardless of their race, ethnicity, or gender.

pathways.name: Work-Life Integration
pathways.def: A measure of the extent to which faculty feel capable of meeting the demands of their role, are able to handle all they are asked to do, and believe that their workload allows for a healthy work/life balance.
pathways.sample: My faculty workload allows me to maintain a healthy work/life balance.

instruments.closing: The online survey also includes measures of satisfaction with pay and benefits, job security, and levels of participation in university committees, leadership roles, and external commitments. Demographic characteristics of the faculty include gender, race/ethnicity, age, marital status, highest degree earned, rank, years at the institution, tenure status, discipline, teaching and advising load, and administrative responsibilities.
instruments.admin: An institution can participate at any time during the year, but national norms are created each November and April. After you complete the online registration, we will send you a custom survey link and a sample email to send to all your full-time faculty. We will send one follow-up email to participants a week after the survey opens. The survey will close after two weeks.

instruments.label: Staff
instruments.name: Staff Thriving Quotient
instruments.description: The Staff Thriving Quotient: what it measures, its scales, how administration works, sample items, and what a campus survey costs.
instruments.capsule: The Staff Thriving Quotient (STQ) is an instrument developed to assess the vital engagement of full-time university staff in their role. The Staff Thriving Quotient is a valid and reliable (α = .93) instrument that assesses staff flourishing in five dimensions: Meaningful Engagement, Institutional Affinity, Accomplishment, Well-Being, and Relationships. Attention to the predictors and campus elements that contribute to staff thriving can enable institutional leaders to retain and support staff.
instruments.scales_intro: The 21 items on the STQ cluster onto 5 scales:

scales.name: Meaningful Engagement
scales.def: A measure of the degree to which staff are energized by their work, feel that their work is a good fit for them, enjoy working for this institution, experience positive emotions at work, and find meaning and purpose in their university role.
scales.sample: I feel energized by my work at this institution.

scales.name: Institutional Affinity
scales.def: A measure of the staff member’s feeling that they are proud to work for this institution, that their values are aligned with the institutional mission, and that they enjoy working for this institution specifically.
scales.sample: I really enjoy working for this institution.

scales.name: Well-Being
scales.def: An indicator of the degree to which one’s workload allows for a healthy work/life balance and that one’s work is not having a negative effect on their physical and/or psychological health.
scales.sample: My workload allows me to maintain a healthy work/life balance.

scales.name: Relationships
scales.def: An indicator of the positive relationships staff have with their coworkers, along with the degree to which they feel supported and valued in those relationships, as well as the degree to which they feel their supervisor cares about them and provides positive feedback.
scales.sample: I feel valued by my colleagues here.

scales.name: Accomplishment
scales.def: An assessment of the degree to which staff feel good about their accomplishments so far, know how to apply their strengths to address work challenges, achieve the goals they set, and believe their work makes a difference in students’ lives.
scales.sample: I feel good about what I have accomplished so far in my role at this institution.

instruments.pathways_intro: Examining thriving among university staff developed out of a desire to understand the working environment that could sustain and retain high-quality staff, so that students were supported and well-served. Dr. Laurie Schreiner developed the Staff Thriving Quotient (STQ) using concepts from positive psychology (e.g., flourishing) and positive organizational scholarship. Staff thriving reflects not only how staff are feeling about their work, but also their relationship to the institution where they work and the ways in which they interact with others in that space that bring joy and a sense of meaning and purpose.
instruments.closing: Research on staff thriving has discovered that there are specific experiences that serve as significant pathways to thriving for university staff. The online instrument assesses these pathways, and they are included in this report. Significant predictors of thriving among university staff include a culture of trust on campus, an equitable working environment, a supervisor who cares, and job security. The instrument also assesses satisfaction with pay and benefits, level of external commitments, and demographic characteristics.
instruments.admin: An institution can participate at any time during the year, but national norms are created each November and April. After you complete the online registration, we will send you a custom survey link and a sample email to send to all your full-time faculty. We will send one follow-up email to participants a week after the survey opens. The survey will close after two weeks.
